tEn: Yann LeCun: The Final Boss of AI
tZh: 杨立昆：AI 的终极 Boss
sEn: In this episode, we welcome Yann LeCun, a pioneer in AI, to discuss his journey, from early neural networks to world models.
sZh: 本期节目，我们邀请到 AI 领域的先驱杨立昆，畅谈他从早期神经网络到世界模型的探索之旅。

consensus.en: The future of AI lies in world models, not generative models, for understanding the physical world.
consensus.zh: AI的未来在于世界模型，而非生成模型，以理解物理世界。

consensus.en: World models require non-generative architectures like JEPA to handle uncertainty in continuous, noisy environments.
consensus.zh: 世界模型需要像JEPA这样的非生成架构来处理连续、嘈杂环境中的不确定性。

consensus.en: Reasoning cannot be achieved through autoregressive token prediction; it requires latent space manipulation.
consensus.zh: 推理不能通过自回归词元预测实现；它需要在潜在空间中进行操作。

consensus.en: Agentic systems without predictive world models are fundamentally flawed and cannot work reliably.
consensus.zh: 没有预测性世界模型的智能体系统存在根本缺陷，无法可靠工作。

consensus.en: Open, federated AI is essential for cultural diversity and democratic sovereignty, avoiding concentration of power.
consensus.zh: 开放、联邦式的AI对于文化多样性和民主主权至关重要，避免权力集中。

contrarian.en: Generative AI should be abandoned for world modeling; it is unsuitable for real-world prediction.
contrarian.zh: 生成式AI应被放弃用于世界建模；它不适合现实世界的预测。

contrarian.en: LLMs are just knowledge repositories, not intelligent; they lack the ability to invent new recipes.
contrarian.zh: LLM只是知识库，而非智能；它们缺乏发明新方法的能力。

contrarian.en: Predicting the next token is not reasoning; true reasoning happens in latent space, not in symbols.
contrarian.zh: 预测下一个词元不是推理；真正的推理发生在潜在空间，而非符号中。

contrarian.en: Contrastive learning methods are ineffective; distillation and regularization like SIGReg are superior.
contrarian.zh: 对比学习方法效率低下；蒸馏和正则化（如SIGReg）更优越。

contrarian.en: Training world models on video games is misguided; real-world data requires non-generative approaches.
contrarian.zh: 在视频游戏上训练世界模型是错误的；现实世界数据需要非生成方法。

contrarian.en: The main danger of AI is not unemployment but the homogenization of culture and bias from a few companies.
contrarian.zh: AI的主要危险不是失业，而是少数公司导致的文化同质化和偏见。

turns.en: Welcome to À LA FRENCH. In this episode, we welcome our last guest of the season. And this guest is a pioneer. He is the leader. He is the final boss. The final boss of AI as we know it today. He is creating today a global platform. He does World Models. And this guest, we will discuss with him for an hour and a half. And exclusively in À LA FRENCH, let's go!
turns.zh: 欢迎来到 À LA FRENCH。本期节目，我们迎来了本季的最后一位嘉宾。这位嘉宾是一位先驱。他是领导者。他是终极 Boss。当今 AI 领域的终极 Boss。他正在打造一个全球平台。他研究世界模型。我们将与他畅谈一个半小时。仅在 À LA FRENCH，我们开始吧！

turns.en: Important announcement. When we announced the À LA FRENCH evening on June 12, in less than 24 hours, the 250 places were sold. So we had a great evening, but hundreds of people couldn't come and were on a waiting list. And we don't like frustration. So we decided to do it again, but bigger, for the À LA FRENCH conference. On December 3, we'll see you there. We will be 1200, coming from all over France to celebrate French tech and a certain vision of tech. We are a nation of engineers. We invented Minitel before the Internet, the TGV before Hyperloops, DivX, X264, VLC, before streaming on Netflix. We are not going to let anyone tell us how we do tech, are we? Come on, the conference that has a certain idea of technology, will be on December 3rd. One day for the YouTube show community, announcement preview, guest rare, gifts, games. And pay attention, this is going to be very French. This is going to be the most incredible tech conference to which you have never attended. And we will celebrate together a certain idea of technology. You can go to alafrench.org right now, reserve your seats with reduced rates for those who cannot afford it and support rates for those who can. So we will meet on December 3rd live. And in the meantime, we're going back to the episode.
turns.zh: 重要公告。当我们宣布 6 月 12 日的 À LA FRENCH 之夜时，不到 24 小时，250 个名额就售罄了。那晚我们度过了一段美好时光，但还有数百人无法到场，只能排队等候。我们不喜欢让人失望。所以我们决定再来一次，但规模更大，那就是 À LA FRENCH 大会。12 月 3 日，我们不见不散。届时将有 1200 人，来自法国各地，共同庆祝法国科技和某种科技愿景。我们是一个工程师的国度。我们在互联网之前发明了 Minitel，在超级高铁之前发明了 TGV，在 Netflix 流媒体之前发明了 DivX、X264、VLC。我们不会让任何人告诉我们该怎么做科技，对吧？来吧，这场有着独特科技理念的大会，将于 12 月 3 日举行。这一天属于 YouTube 节目社区，有预告发布、稀有嘉宾、礼物和游戏。请注意，这将非常法国。这将是你从未参加过的最不可思议的科技大会。我们将共同庆祝某种科技理念。你现在就可以访问 alafrench.org 预订座位，负担不起的人有优惠价，负担得起的人有支持价。我们 12 月 3 日现场见。与此同时，我们回到节目。

turns.en: We are in À LA FRENCH and you know the game. To guess the guest, in 4 points, if you know it immediately, 3 points if you need hints, 2 points if you need more hints, and 1 point when everything has already been said. Are you ready to play, Steve?
turns.zh: 我们在 À LA FRENCH，你知道游戏规则。猜嘉宾，4 个提示点：如果你立刻知道，得 3 分；如果需要提示，得 2 分；如果需要更多提示，得 1 分；当所有提示都说完时，得 0 分。你准备好玩了吗，Steve？

turns.en: I'm ready. Ready for what? Me, I'm going to win.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。准备好什么？我，我会赢。

turns.en: Okay, let's go. So, in 4 points. Our guest is an extremely well-known researcher. No, we're joking. It's Yann LeCun.
turns.zh: 好，我们开始。所以，4 个提示点。我们的嘉宾是一位极其著名的研究者。不，我们开玩笑的。是 Yann LeCun。

turns.en: Okay, we won't waste any time. Welcome, Yann.
turns.zh: 好，我们不浪费时间了。欢迎，Yann。

turns.en: It's a pleasure to be here. Thank you for inviting me.
turns.zh: 很高兴来到这里。谢谢你们的邀请。

turns.en: In addition, Neon Noir is a place you know. You come here from time to time, when you come to France.
turns.zh: 而且，Neon Noir 是你熟悉的地方。你来法国时，会时不时来这里。

turns.en: Yes, 2-3 times, I've already been here. It's changed a lot. It's become populated, furnished, expanded.
turns.zh: 是的，我来过两三次了。这里变化很大。变得热闹了，布置好了，扩大了。

turns.en: You know with Yann for longer than we do. Since the very beginning of ZML. We were introduced by Gabriel. By Gabriel Synnaeve.
turns.zh: 你认识 Yann 比我们更久。从 ZML 一开始就认识了。我们是 Gabriel 介绍的。Gabriel Synnaeve。

turns.en: And then, for the story, we got into it, got into it in the sense... "Heyyyy !" We got into a fight. We got into a fight about programming languages.
turns.zh: 然后，说到故事，我们陷入了，陷入了那种……“嘿！”我们吵起来了。我们为编程语言吵起来了。

turns.en: Yes. And in particular, what is called multi-stage programming. So, referring to a language called Terra, which was a kind of super set of Lua. Yes. So, the idea is to have metaprogramming in the language. You see, actually, you have only one control flow. where you program the language using the language itself. In contrast to a macro, or a template, or all metaprogramming.
turns.zh: 是的。特别是所谓的多阶段编程。指的是叫 Terra 的语言，它是 Lua 的一种超集。是的。所以，想法是在语言中实现元编程。你看，实际上，你只有一个控制流。你用语言本身来编程语言。与宏、模板或所有元编程相对。

turns.en: And so, he had told me... "ah!!" And I see you too, Yann, every time, because whenever Steve makes a very Frenchmaxing tweet, with raclette or things like that, in Savoie, all of that, there's a little like from Yann LeCun. That's kind of it. I can always count on it.
turns.zh: 所以，他告诉我……“啊！！”而且我也看到你，Yann，每次，因为每当 Steve 发一条非常 Frenchmaxing 的推文，比如奶酪火锅或类似的东西，在萨瓦省，所有这些，都会有 Yann LeCun 的一个小赞。就是这样。我总能指望上。

turns.en: At first, I was happy. I looked. Now, I said yes. Is that, the French Maxing?
turns.zh: 起初，我很高兴。我看了。现在，我说是的。这就是 French Maxing 吗？

turns.en: Frenchmaxxing, it's nothing now. It's a maximization of France. Maximization. As Victor Hugo said, who used, I don't know what word, then someone told him: "But that's not a French word." He said, "Well, now, if." It's still cool to be called Hugo when you can define what. The dictionary, it's me.
turns.zh: Frenchmaxxing，现在什么都不是了。这是法国的最大化。最大化。正如维克多·雨果所说，他用了某个词，然后有人告诉他：“但这不是法语词。”他说：“嗯，现在，如果。”当你能够定义什么时，被称为雨果仍然很酷。字典，就是我。

turns.en: But this discussion, the reason for which we had discussed this, is because I am a big fan of LISP. And LISP, it's a language...
turns.zh: 但这次讨论，我们讨论这个的原因，是因为我是 LISP 的忠实粉丝。而 LISP，它是一种语言……

turns.en: Exactly. Data is code.
turns.zh: 正是。数据即代码。

turns.en: Yes, data is code, and then you can tinker. It's a programmable programming language. There are a lot of parentheses that we're going to use. That's not a problem. Me, I've never been able to get used to it. Is that true? I've done a lot of closures. Were you an Emacs guy?
turns.zh: 是的，数据即代码，然后你可以修补。它是一种可编程的编程语言。我们会用到很多括号。那没问题。我，我一直没能习惯。真的吗？我写过很多闭包。你是 Emacs 用户吗？

turns.en: No, but in Emacs, I was a customer. I wasn't a programmer at Emacs. However, when I did a lot of Clojure, which I love, in fact, pushed by someone who is called Pierre-Yves Ritschard who is the CTO of Poolside, now. I really felt like I was creating a language, you see, a language of the future. Finally, somewhere in the past, since syntax is all that matters. It's a bit in the past. But damn, I've never managed to get it right. Parentheses, they make me... I did everything, the colorings, the gadgets and all that. I've never managed to get it right.
turns.zh: 不，但在 Emacs 里，我是用户。我不是 Emacs 的程序员。然而，当我写了很多 Clojure 时，我其实很喜欢，事实上，是被一个叫 Pierre-Yves Ritschard 的人推动的，他现在是 Poolside 的 CTO。我真的觉得我在创造一种语言，你看，一种未来的语言。最终，在过去的某个地方，因为语法才是最重要的。这有点过时。但该死，我一直没能搞定。括号，它们让我……我做了所有事情，着色、小工具等等。我一直没能搞定。

transcript.sec: Léon Bottou and the LISP interpreter

turns.en: And a little known fact, in 87, when I finished my doctorate, I met a young student from polytechnique called Léon Botou. Oh! And then, he said, I would like to do a project for my final year at Polytechnique. Will I do an internship with you? I told him, you can't, because I haven't finished my thesis. It's not a problem, I won't tell the school. And I told him, well, listen, I'm starting to write a new neural network simulator. Do you want to help me? And I said, I would really like to have an interface language. I thought about using Forth and things like that. Instead of inventing a language, it might actually be a LISP. So, I would really like a LISP interpreter. And we both had Amiga 1000s.
turns.zh: 还有一个鲜为人知的事实，87 年，当我完成博士学位时，我遇到了一个叫 Léon Bottou 的 polytechnique 年轻学生。哦！然后，他说，他想在 polytechnique 的最后一年做一个项目。我能跟你实习吗？我告诉他，你不能，因为我还没完成论文。没问题，我不会告诉学校的。我告诉他，嗯，听着，我开始写一个新的神经网络模拟器。你想帮我吗？我说，我真的很想要一个接口语言。我考虑过用 Forth 之类的东西。与其发明一种语言，不如用 LISP。所以，我真的很想要一个 LISP 解释器。我们俩都有 Amiga 1000。

turns.en: I see that you don't have one on your table here. But that's a shame.
turns.zh: 我看到你这里桌上没有一台。真可惜。

turns.en: Yes, next time, that will be fixed. But anyway, I didn't insult you, I brought you a BeBox.
turns.zh: 是的，下次会补上。但不管怎样，我没侮辱你，我给你带了一台 BeBox。

turns.en: A BeBox. But actually, the BeBox is a copy of the Amiga. Exactly. There you go. And you did it on purpose, of course.
turns.zh: 一台 BeBox。但实际上，BeBox 是 Amiga 的复制品。正是。就是这样。当然，你是故意的。

turns.en: So no, but we have a conversation on Twitter, actually. Yann had bounced back and actually, he had explained. Maybe it's a bit difficult to find Amigas today, right? Less than BeBoxes, I can tell you. That one... You can find emulators and all that. But you can also buy them.
turns.zh: 所以不，但我们在 Twitter 上有过对话，实际上。Yann 回复了，实际上，他解释过。也许现在找 Amiga 有点难，对吧？比 BeBox 少，我可以告诉你。那个……你可以找到模拟器之类的。但你也可以买到。

turns.en: And Léon, in three weeks, wrote a tablet-list in C, which I used as a front-end. Then, I went to do my postdoc in Toronto. And actually, we used that system, which initially was called SN, Simulateur Neuronal, which later became Lush, when we open-sourced it in 2002. And I used it in all my research with my students until 2011, where then we switched to Torch. In Lua, so. So, it was based on Lua and then, PyTorch, but that was much later. So, there was a long lifespan. There were successive versions.
turns.zh: Léon 在三个星期内，用 C 语言写了一个表格列表，我把它用作前端。然后，我去多伦多做博士后。实际上，我们用了那个系统，最初叫 SN，Simulateur Neuronal，后来在 2002 年开源时改名为 Lush。我一直用它和我的学生做研究，直到 2011 年，然后我们转向了 Torch。用 Lua。所以，它基于 Lua，然后是 PyTorch，但那要晚得多。所以，它寿命很长。有连续版本。

turns.en: What were we following? It was written about backpropagation, multi-layer networks, etc. justement, the backpropagation of the gradient, is a bit the foundation of how today, the learning engine neural networks is a bit based on that. Already, back then, your thesis, it's about the core of neural networks. So, what is it? Is it 87, the end of the thesis?
turns.zh: 我们当时在关注什么？它写的是反向传播、多层网络等。正是，梯度的反向传播，有点像是今天神经网络学习引擎的基础。早在当时，你的论文，就是关于神经网络的核心。那么，是什么？是 87 年，论文结束的时候吗？

turns.en: For the few Padawans who haven't yet... Are you born? Just, just, just.
turns.zh: 对于那些还没……你出生了吗？刚刚，刚刚，刚刚。

turns.en: But then, you go to Bell Labs, right?
turns.zh: 但然后，你去了贝尔实验室，对吧？

turns.en: No, first, I do a postdoc at the University of Toronto with Jeff Hinton.
turns.zh: 不，首先，我在多伦多大学和 Jeff Hinton 做博士后。

turns.en: Ah yes, okay.
turns.zh: 啊，是的，好的。

turns.en: No, and after, I went to Bell Labs in late 88.
turns.zh: 不，之后我于 88 年底去了贝尔实验室。

turns.en: Okay, you stayed there for 15 years, right, approximately?
turns.zh: 好的，你在那里待了大约 15 年，对吧？

turns.en: So, 12 years at AT&T. Bell Labs is the research lab of AT&T. It later changed its name because AT&T split up, but about a dozen years.
turns.zh: 所以在 AT&T 待了 12 年。贝尔实验室是 AT&T 的研究实验室。后来因为 AT&T 分拆而改名，但大约 12 年。

turns.en: And it is there that you really matured and developed convolutional neural networks, right?
turns.zh: 正是在那里，你真正成熟并发展了卷积神经网络，对吗？

turns.en: Yes, yes. I had already started in Toronto. And even in my thesis, I had networks with local connections and all that. So, it was already a bit there. But yes, that's where we actually did it.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。我在多伦多就已经开始了。甚至在我的论文里，我就有了局部连接的网络等等。所以，那已经有点雏形了。但确实，我们是在那里真正做出来的。

turns.en: And then, Léon, on his side, was doing a thesis in France. And he made it work for speech recognition. He also worked on convolutional networks. And we ended up making products that used convolutional networks for reading checks, things like that.
turns.zh: 然后，Léon 在法国做论文。他把它用在了语音识别上。他也研究了卷积网络。我们最终做出了使用卷积网络读取支票等产品的产品。

turns.en: The applications... Yes, for letters, addresses.
turns.zh: 应用……是的，用于信件、地址。

turns.en: Yes, addresses, it has never been a commercial thing. It was a prototype.
turns.zh: 是的，地址，那从来不是商业化的东西。那是一个原型。

turns.en: Ah yes? Ah okay.
turns.zh: 啊，是吗？啊，好的。

turns.en: But the commercial applications, the main one, was for reading amounts on checks and things like that, financial documents. Yes, reports on you, really, where we do the recognition of alphanumeric signs and everything. It's really for checks. And that had a commercial life between the mid-1990s and early 2000s.
turns.zh: 但商业应用，主要的，是读取支票上的金额等等，金融文件。是的，真的，我们做字母数字符号的识别等等。那真的是为了支票。那在 1990 年代中期到 2000 年代初有商业生命。

turns.en: But I was no longer involved. Because from 1996, in fact, AT&T separated. And then, it was the early years of the Internet. And the part of AT&T that commercialized these systems of reading checks, in fact, was separated from us. And the patents belonged to them.
turns.zh: 但我不再参与了。因为从 1996 年起，事实上 AT&T 分拆了。然后，那是互联网的早期。AT&T 中商业化这些支票读取系统的部分，事实上，从我们这里分离出去了。专利属于他们。

turns.en: And where, physically? In New Jersey.
turns.zh: 那物理上在哪里？在新泽西。

turns.en: And so, you stayed in New Jersey, 2003-2013, is that right, New York University, NYU?
turns.zh: 所以，你待在新泽西，2003 到 2013 年，对吗，纽约大学，NYU？

turns.en: I spent a short time at the NEC Research Institute, in the large Japanese company, NEC. And then, that lab, it kind of fell apart. So, I left pretty quickly and I became a professor at NYU in 2003.
turns.zh: 我在 NEC 研究所待了一小段时间，那是日本大公司 NEC。然后，那个实验室有点解体了。所以我很快就离开了，并在 2003 年成为 NYU 的教授。

turns.en: And ten years later, 2013, I joined Facebook. But part-time, I was still a professor. I am still a professor at NYU.
turns.zh: 十年后，2013 年，我加入了 Facebook。但兼职，我仍然是教授。我仍然是 NYU 的教授。

transcript.secZh: 早期职业生涯与贝尔实验室

turns.en: Actually, it's quite interesting because the world of academic research and the world of research in the company are quite linked. In any case, and me, sometimes, I think, is this the world, the open source, or in any case, the free sharing of information, of research, is this not what drives, what sometimes obliges companies to keep a foot in publications or in this kind of things?
turns.zh: 实际上，这很有趣，因为学术研究界和公司研究界联系紧密。无论如何，我有时想，这个世界，开源，或者无论如何，信息的自由共享，研究的自由共享，难道不是推动公司有时必须在出版物或这类事情上保持一席之地的原因吗？

turns.en: No, in fact, what drives in large part… No, the direct, the bar. What drives companies in large part to have relationships with the university, in any case, in the United States, is access to talent. That is, they want to have a pipeline, you see, of interns, to have a relationship with professors who are working on subjects that interest them, because you are a good student who could come and work for us, and teach us how to use your methods, etc. So, it's a really good reason for the relationship.
turns.zh: 不，事实上，很大程度上驱动……不，直接的，门槛。在美国，很大程度上驱动公司与大学建立关系的是获取人才。也就是说，他们想要一个实习生管道，与那些研究他们感兴趣课题的教授建立关系，因为你是一个好学生，可以来为我们工作，教我们如何使用你的方法等等。所以，这是建立关系的真正好理由。

turns.en: And in the United States, doctoral students, for example, so there is no equivalent to the numbers that there are in France. Where doctoral students can do this on-site, in industry. There is no such thing in the United States. But on the other hand, the three months of summer, students can do whatever they want. So, they are not tied to the university. And most of them will do internships in industry. And so, they are a bit like the bees of American technology. Because you need to circulate ideas, techniques.
turns.zh: 在美国，例如博士生，没有像法国那样的数量。在法国，博士生可以在工业界现场做这些。在美国没有这种事。但另一方面，三个月的夏天，学生可以做任何他们想做的事。所以，他们不受大学束缚。他们中的大多数人会在工业界实习。所以，他们有点像美国技术的蜜蜂。因为你需要传播思想、技术。

turns.en: And one of the things you are also known for, is that you created the Lab Le Faire, Facebook AI Research. You are trying to promote the American model, there.
turns.zh: 而且你还有一件出名的事，就是你创建了 FAIR 实验室，Facebook AI Research。你在那里试图推广美国模式。

turns.en: But no, and in fact, honestly, today, I don't know, half of the ecosystem, well, a good part of the French ecosystem in AI, are from Fer. Anyway, there is a, clearly, Fer mafia. So, there are quite a few researchers and engineers who have passed through Fer, who then went on to found boxes, etc. or began to work in other labs.
turns.zh: 但不，事实上，老实说，今天，我不知道，一半的生态系统，嗯，法国 AI 生态系统的很大一部分，来自 FAIR。无论如何，显然有一个 FAIR 黑手党。所以，有相当多的研究人员和工程师经历过 FAIR，然后去创办公司等等，或者开始在其他实验室工作。

turns.en: But there is also the fact that fer had a cruising speed until last year. It had about forty doctoral students in residence. So, since the doctorate lasts three years, that means there were about twelve each year, who had completed their doctorate at Fer with access to computing resources, etc. with access to the best researchers in the field and everything. And so, all these people, of course, have completely disrupted the ecosystem.
turns.zh: 但还有一个事实，FAIR 直到去年都有巡航速度。它有大约 40 名常驻博士生。所以，由于博士持续三年，这意味着每年大约有 12 人，他们在 FAIR 完成了博士，获得了计算资源等，接触了该领域最好的研究人员等等。所以，这些人，当然，完全颠覆了生态系统。

turns.en: I think that the creation of FAIR Paris in 2015 had a huge effect on the French ecosystem, finally, Parisian, in particular French, in general and in Europe, in fact. So, it gave ideas to talented young students that, in fact, to do a doctorate in AI, it's the coolest thing they could imagine. Fifteen years ago, the coolest thing that people were doing young students who were graduating from school, it's about doing the finances. And that has changed. It's no longer about finance now, it's about AI.
turns.zh: 我认为 2015 年 FAIR Paris 的创建对法国生态系统产生了巨大影响，最终，巴黎，特别是法国，总体上，事实上还有欧洲。所以，它给了有才华的年轻学生一个想法，事实上，攻读 AI 博士是他们能想象的最酷的事情。十五年前，年轻学生从学校毕业时做的最酷的事情是搞金融。那已经改变了。现在不再是金融，而是 AI。

turns.en: We had received Neil Zeghidour, who told us they wanted to do a thesis and in short, they hadn't necessarily been taken, but he was told, listen, there is this thesis...
turns.zh: 我们接待过 Neil Zeghidour，他告诉我们他们想做论文，总之，他们不一定被录取了，但有人告诉他，听着，有这篇论文……

turns.en: No, no, it's the opposite. They wanted to write a thesis on neural networks, at the time, and there were so few, it hadn't even returned to Hype, what they told him, well, listen, if you're really interested, go ahead. Then, finally, actually, it was...
turns.zh: 不，不，恰恰相反。他们当时想写关于神经网络的论文，而且很少，甚至还没回到炒作期，他们告诉他，嗯，听着，如果你真的感兴趣，就去做吧。然后，最后，实际上，那是……

turns.en: You, you had seen that 40 years ago, but...
turns.zh: 你，你 40 年前就看到了，但……

turns.en: Yes, no, but it's true that there was a period phase for the neuron zone between the end of the 1980s and the mid-1990s. Then, everyone lost interest. It became a bit taboo. And it has somewhat reappeared at the end of the 2000s because of the media battle we had with Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton. The deep learning, you know. We renamed this deep learning and then we mainly proposed new methods. Then we finally made it work too. And so, it finally convinced the communities initially, speech recognition, then, image recognition, of course. And then, thirdly, the understanding of natural language, what, NLP, that deep learning, was really something that worked. So, it revolutionized these three fields.
turns.zh: 是的，不，但确实在 1980 年代末到 1990 年代中期，神经领域有一个阶段。然后，每个人都失去了兴趣。它变得有点禁忌。它在 2000 年代末重新出现，部分是因为我们与 Yoshua Bengio 和 Geoffrey Hinton 的媒体战。深度学习，你知道。我们重新命名了它，然后我们主要提出了新方法。然后我们最终也让它成功了。所以，它最终说服了社区，最初是语音识别，然后当然是图像识别。然后第三，自然语言理解，NLP，深度学习确实有效。所以，它彻底改变了这三个领域。

turns.en: But it's true that in France, in the academic environment, in 2015, there were practically no one doing it in universities. They were still... Academics are a bit conservative. And then, in France, we like maths and deep learning, it's not easy to do math, you know. It's not easier if we use methods, like kernel methods, Bayesian stuff, all that. One can do beautiful math. It doesn't work as well, but... Well, we can write books. But it's beautiful math, you know. But these are beautiful mathematics.
turns.zh: 但确实，在法国，在学术界，2015 年，大学里几乎没有人做这个。他们仍然……学者有点保守。然后，在法国，我们喜欢数学，而深度学习不容易做数学，你知道。如果我们使用方法，比如核方法、贝叶斯之类，也不容易。可以做漂亮的数学。它效果不太好，但……嗯，我们可以写书。但那是漂亮的数学，你知道。但那是漂亮的数学。

turns.en: How is it that this has become a bit obsolete, but that there was less interest starting from the early 2000s?
turns.zh: 怎么会变得有点过时，但从 2000 年代初开始兴趣就减少了？

turns.en: No, it's rather the mid-1990s.
turns.zh: 不，更确切地说是 1990 年代中期。

turns.en: Mid-1990s, what is it due to? Because it was too complicated? Did it require too much power?
turns.zh: 1990 年代中期，是什么原因？因为它太复杂？需要太多算力？

turns.en: There are many reasons. I'm not the best person to analyze that, because I was right in the middle of it, but I think there are a combination of reasons.
turns.zh: 有很多原因。我不是分析这个的最佳人选，因为我就在其中，但我认为有各种原因的组合。

turns.en: The first is that it was indeed complicated, and there were no software tools, portable ones, etc., that people used. Everyone used completely different computer platforms. You couldn't do a neural network on PCs; it's not possible. It was either Sun workstations, Silicon Graphics, or proprietary systems like IRIX, AIX, HPUX, and so on. So we were under Sun, then we switched to Silicon Graphics because they had better performance at the time. And there wasn't the software, there wasn't Python, there weren't all those open-source gadgets we can use now. The only open-source tools were things like GCC, Emacs, and others, but not really for that. So actually, with Léon, we had written a complete system with a LISP interpreter, along with a LISP compiler and all that. But we couldn't really exchange our software. There was no platform, no SourceForge, no GitHub, no Internet. That came later. So in fact, everyone had to invest six months to a year to create a platform to make neural networks work. Most people made mistakes because it's very easy to do silly things when implementing backprop for the first time—like an hour of sign language or something. So it was a big investment for people, and most didn't want to do that. So what did they do? They used MATLAB and did something simple, but building a neural network with MATLAB at the time wasn't really possible. There really weren't the tools, except for people who invested time in the tools. What we did with Léon—that's what gave us superpowers—was that we made our own tools.
turns.zh: 首先，这确实很复杂，而且没有人们使用的软件工具、便携工具等等。每个人使用的计算机平台完全不同。在 PC 上做神经网络是不可能的。要么是 Sun 工作站，要么是 Silicon Graphics，要么是专有系统，比如 IRIX、AIX、HPUX 等等。所以我们当时用 Sun，后来转到 Silicon Graphics，因为那时它们的性能更好。而且没有软件，没有 Python，没有我们现在能用的那些开源小工具。唯一的开源工具是像 GCC、Emacs 之类的东西，但并不是真正用于这个的。所以实际上，我和 Léon 写了一个完整的系统，带有一个 LISP 解释器，同时还有一个 LISP 编译器等等。但我们真的无法交换我们的软件。没有平台，没有 SourceForge，没有 GitHub，没有互联网。那是后来才有的。所以事实上，每个人都要投入六个月到一年的时间来创建一个平台来让神经网络工作。大多数人都会犯错，因为第一次实现反向传播时很容易做蠢事——比如花一个小时做手语之类的事。所以这对人们来说是一个巨大的投入，大多数人不想这么做。那他们做什么呢？他们用 MATLAB 做一些简单的东西，但当时用 MATLAB 构建神经网络真的不可能。真的没有工具，除了那些投入时间做工具的人。我和 Léon 所做的——那就是给我们超能力的地方——是我们自己做了工具。

turns.en: And this allowed us to make convolutional networks and see how they worked, with a whole graphical library for visualization and everything, which was actually more powerful than what we have today. In fact, it's amazing. And so it meant that there was no communication like there is now, which is instantaneous, where you download the latest code associated with a paper and you can run the latest network. Back then, one had to spend six months or a year to implement something. So it really was necessary to believe in it. That means you had the garbage, and you would reimplement cleanroom the papers. There were people who wanted to reimplement convolutional networks. There weren't many. And there was this legend that I was more or less the only one who knew how to make them work, which was completely wrong. But it wasn't that complicated. But it's true that it required tools.
turns.zh: 这让我们能够制作卷积网络，并看到它们是如何工作的，还有一个完整的图形库用于可视化等等，这实际上比我们今天拥有的还要强大。事实上，这很惊人。所以这意味着没有像现在这样的即时通信，你可以下载与论文相关的最新代码，然后运行最新的网络。那时，人们必须花六个月或一年来实现一些东西。所以真的需要相信它。这意味着你有垃圾，你会按照论文重新实现。有人想重新实现卷积网络，但不多。而且有这样一个传说，我或多或少是唯一一个知道如何让它们工作的人，这完全是错误的。但这并不复杂。不过确实需要工具。

turns.en: At the same time, it's the name. Yann le qu'un. You see, we believe there's only one. There's only one. But that means you had people above you, in management at Bell Labs, etc., who believed in it, after all, and who weren't afraid to have the means, the time, for all that? The way Bell Labs operated. So, the director of the lab, a guy named Larry Jackel, who had created the group in 1985, I think, based on neural networks. In fact, he's a physicist by profession. And then he had a new department, so he wondered what to do. Because at Bell Labs, we hired intelligent people, we gave them the means to succeed, and we gave them peace. OK. It's cool, that. If he was asking for resources, obviously, he was asking questions. But basically, we let people work on what they wanted. So he went completely off track and asked on what I would have worked, what is the cool thing. And he met John Hopfield, who was a professor at Princeton, but who had a part-time job at Bell Labs. It was between Princeton and Caltech. And he asked me on what I would have worked. And John Hopfield said to him that he was a physicist, that he was working on hardware for neural networks, special chips for making neural networks. This concept is not new. John Hopfield, a Nobel laureate in physics with Geoffrey Hinton two years ago for what are called Hopfield and Geoffrey networks, and Boltzmann machines. It was originally a biophysicist. And so Larry got into that. He hired a few people. And then I came in in '88. And then I started working on convolutional networks pretty quickly, because I had already worked on that in Toronto. They had character-based databases. And so, in two months, I was there. I beat all the performance records on the character-based things.
turns.zh: 同时，这就是名字。Yann le qu'un。你看，我们相信只有一个。只有一个。但这意味着你上面的人，比如贝尔实验室的管理层，他们毕竟相信这一点，并且不害怕拥有手段、时间等等？贝尔实验室的运作方式就是这样。所以，实验室主任，一个叫 Larry Jackel 的人，他在 1985 年创建了这个小组，我想是基于神经网络的。事实上，他是一名物理学家。然后他有了一个新的部门，所以他不知道该怎么办。因为在贝尔实验室，我们雇佣聪明的人，给他们成功的手段，给他们安宁。好的。这很酷。如果他要求资源，显然，他在问问题。但基本上，我们让人们做他们想做的事。所以他完全偏离了轨道，问我我会做什么，什么是酷的事情。他遇到了 John Hopfield，他是普林斯顿的教授，但在贝尔实验室兼职。他在普林斯顿和加州理工之间。他问我我会做什么。John Hopfield 告诉他，他是一名物理学家，他在研究神经网络的硬件，用于制造神经网络的特殊芯片。这个概念并不新鲜。John Hopfield，两年前与 Geoffrey Hinton 一起获得诺贝尔物理学奖，因为所谓的 Hopfield 和 Geoffrey 网络，以及玻尔兹曼机。他最初是一名生物物理学家。所以 Larry 对此产生了兴趣。他雇了几个人。然后我在 88 年加入。然后我很快就开始研究卷积网络，因为我在多伦多已经做过这个。他们有基于字符的数据库。所以，两个月后，我就在那里了。我打破了所有基于字符的东西的性能记录。

turns.en: And there was something, a funny story, it was that before... When I was still a post-doc in Toronto, Larry Jackel asked me, "Listen, you're coming in October, we'd like to order a computer for you, so that you can work when you arrive, that it's there when you arrive. What do you use at the moment?" I said, "We use a Sun 4, there's one that just arrived in Toronto, it's great, all of that, it's a huge flop, it's hallucinatory." He says, "Ok." And then, it was a Sun 4 which was the central server of the entire IT department.
turns.zh: 还有一件事，一个有趣的故事，那是在之前……当我还在多伦多做博士后时，Larry Jackel 问我：“听着，你十月份来，我们想为你订购一台电脑，这样你到达时就能工作，它在你到达时就在那里。你现在用什么？”我说：“我们用 Sun 4，多伦多刚到了一台，很棒，所有的一切，它是个巨大的成功，令人难以置信。”他说：“好的。”然后，那是一台 Sun 4，是整个 IT 部门的中央服务器。

turns.en: Ah, so everyone was on a mainframe?
turns.zh: 啊，所以大家都在主机上？

turns.en: It wasn't a mainframe, that's what we called a mini-computer. It is a mini-computer.
turns.zh: 那不是主机，我们称之为小型机。那是一台小型机。

turns.en: Ah, but you mean everyone was involved? Everyone would be on it.
turns.zh: 啊，但你的意思是所有人都参与？所有人都会在上面。

turns.en: You had 30 or 40 doctoral students who were connecting to that thing. Not everyone used it for neural networks, but it wasn't really...
turns.zh: 有三四十个博士生连接到那个东西上。不是每个人都用它做神经网络，但它并不是真的……

turns.en: Was it a timeshare?
turns.zh: 那是分时系统吗？

turns.en: It was a unique system, you connect. So, that's the project I was working on. I also had a workstation Sun, but Sun 3 with a 68000. Amazing. So, I said to him, "Okay, Sun 4, it's the one with the Sparc." The Sparc processors of Sun. And I arrive at Bell Labs, and there is a Sun 4, but just for me! That means a lot. That means a lot of things, the methods we use. So, well, I'm a bit skeptical and then I look at Larry. And then he says, smiling, "You know, at Bell Labs, you don't become famous by saving money." There's a lot to learn from that. "You don't get famous by saving money."
turns.zh: 那是一个独特的系统，你连接上去。所以，那是我正在做的项目。我也有一个 Sun 工作站，但是 Sun 3，带 68000。太棒了。所以，我对他说：“好的，Sun 4，就是带 Sparc 的那个。”Sun 的 Sparc 处理器。我到了贝尔实验室，那里有一台 Sun 4，但只给我一个人用！这意义重大。这意义重大，我们使用的方法。所以，我有点怀疑，然后我看着 Larry。然后他笑着说：“你知道，在贝尔实验室，你不会因为省钱而出名。”有很多东西可以从中学习。“你不会因为省钱而出名。”

turns.en: Ah, yes, okay. It's very interesting.
turns.zh: 啊，是的，好的。这非常有趣。

turns.en: So, if we go back a little to return a little more contemporary, but therefore 2013-2023, that is... 2025, no? 2025, it's the era at Meta. You received the Turing Award in 2018, which is the Fields medal or the Nobel Prize in computer science, let's just say so. Right. But, so, at that time, the World Models, there were already two hypotheses between LLMs and World Models. Does that make sense?
turns.zh: 所以，如果我们稍微回到更当代一点，但因此是 2013-2023，那是……2025，不是吗？2025，那是 Meta 的时代。你在 2018 年获得了图灵奖，那是计算机科学领域的菲尔兹奖或诺贝尔奖，就这么说吧。对。但是，所以，在那个时候，世界模型，在 LLM 和世界模型之间已经有了两种假设。这有意义吗？

turns.en: Yes, in a way. Me, for example, I gave a keynote at NIPS. It was still called NIPS at the time, not yet NeurIPS, in 2016. My main message at the end of the speech was: The future of AI is World Models. So, learning predictive models of the world, I think, is the key. And then learning actions and then optimizing intrinsic objective functions are really the path forward for making progress in AI. They are systems that are able to predict what the effect of an action on the world will be, etc., that can be learned in an autonomous way, and then controlled by giving them an objective, etc. So, I had this idea a long time ago. That's even from 2016, it's from before.
turns.zh: 是的，在某种程度上。比如我，我在 NIPS 上做了一个主题演讲。那时它还叫 NIPS，还不是 NeurIPS，在 2016 年。我演讲结尾的主要信息是：AI 的未来是世界模型。所以，学习世界的预测模型，我认为，是关键。然后学习行动，然后优化内在目标函数，确实是 AI 取得进展的前进道路。它们是能够预测一个行动对世界的影响的系统等等，可以以自主的方式学习，然后通过给它们一个目标来控制，等等。所以，我很早就有这个想法。那甚至是从 2016 年开始的，甚至更早。

transcript.sec: Introduction to JEPA and World Models

turns.en: But let's say, I started talking about it publicly, if you want, at that time. But the research hadn't been successful to... If you want, we couldn't really do that in articles because it was still just an idea. And then, for several years, I have had research projects both at Meta and at NYU, to train models which could have been world models through video prediction. In fact, it never worked. So, we tried to make it work until, I don't know, 2021, something like that. Generative models for video prediction. It never worked as a model of the world, in fact, to predict what will happen. Maybe to create generations of videos, but even at that time, it didn't work because we didn't have the diffusion models or anything like that.
turns.zh: 但比如说，我当时开始公开谈论它，如果你愿意的话。但研究还没有成功到……如果你愿意，我们不能在文章里真正写这个，因为它还只是一个想法。然后，好几年里，我在 Meta 和 NYU 都有研究项目，训练那些本可以通过视频预测成为世界模型的模型。事实上，它从未成功过。所以，我们一直试图让它成功，直到，我不知道，2021 年左右。用于视频预测的生成模型。它作为世界模型从未成功过，事实上，去预测将要发生的事情。也许可以生成视频，但即使在那个时候，它也不成功，因为我们还没有扩散模型或类似的东西。

turns.en: Therefore, according to you, because it's just a bad representation of the world, right?
turns.zh: 因此，按照你的说法，因为它只是对世界的糟糕表征，对吧？

turns.en: No, it's the fact that most of the information in a video is unpredictable. The bulk of the information in a video is unpredictable. If I take, here, the people who are watching see only a small part of the room, they may have a vague idea of the surroundings if you turn the camera, but you cannot predict the details, you cannot say that, outside the camera's field of view, there is a video game that is in the process of... little dinosaurs dancing. There is a T-Rex, etc. There are all the people with security here. There is no way you can predict all the details at the pixel level of what is in the video if the camera starts to turn. Who could have predicted? The vast majority of the information in a video or in any real-world signal is unpredictable. So, if we try to train a generative model to hallucinate that is not predictable, it doesn't work very well at the end. And therefore, the crucial idea on which we are working for world models called JEPA, Joint Intermediate Predictive Architecture, in French, predictive architecture of joint hunting.
turns.zh: 不，事实是视频中的大部分信息是不可预测的。视频中的大部分信息是不可预测的。如果我在这里，观看的人只看到房间的一小部分，如果你转动摄像机，他们可能对周围环境有一个模糊的概念，但你无法预测细节，你不能说，在摄像机视野之外，有一个视频游戏正在进行……小恐龙在跳舞。有一只霸王龙，等等。这里还有所有安保人员。如果摄像机开始转动，你根本无法预测视频中像素级别的所有细节。谁能预测到呢？视频或任何现实世界信号中的绝大多数信息是不可预测的。所以，如果我们试图训练一个生成模型去幻觉那些不可预测的东西，最终效果不会很好。因此，我们正在研究的世界模型的关键思想叫做 JEPA，联合中间预测架构，法语里是“联合狩猎的预测架构”。

turns.en: It's nice. Joint hunting. What are you doing, hunting? No, that's beautiful. It's beautiful, it's beautiful.
turns.zh: 这很好。联合狩猎。你在做什么，打猎吗？不，这很美。很美，很美。

turns.en: So, the idea of that, is that we train a system to find an abstract representation of the input signal, let's say, the video, that contains the information that we can predict and which eliminates all the things that we cannot predict. And that, is absolutely crucial for a whole bunch of reasons. We can come back to that if you want, but it's a bit technical or philosophical. So, that's the idea of JEPA, it's nothing else. So, this replaces a generative architecture that predicts everything, in fact, everything. And for discrete tokens, it works because it's easy managing uncertainty in forecasting. All the space is finite. You only have a finite number of tokens, you can predict a probability for each possible token and then, through autoregressive prediction, have a not-so-bad estimate of a probability of a sequence.
